newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope spends moments of silence at parents' grave.
newsitem.headline: Pope spends moments of silence at parents' grave.

text.p: Pope John Paul prayed in silence on Monday at the tomb in Poland of his mother, father and brother whose loss before he was 21 still hurts him deeply.
The 77-year-old Pontiff knelt for several minutes in Krakow's Rakowicki cemetery, head cupped in hands, gazing at the names of those he held dearest engraved on the grey and white marble crypt.
Then he rose and stood a while longer in meditation.
The first part of the penultimate day of the Pope's 11-day Polish trip was devoted to people and places that shaped his youth.
The Pope's mother Emilia died in 1929 when he was eight, leaving him devastated.

When the young Karol Wojtyla was a student in the splendid south Poland city of Krakow in 1939, he wrote of her in his anguished poem the "White Grave": "Oh, how many years have gone by Without You -- how many years?"
His brother Edmund, a recently qualified doctor, fell victim to scarlet fever caught from a patient in 1932.
Then his retired army officer father Karol, who brought him up, died in 1941 after two years of Nazi occupation of their homeland during World War Two.
Each visit to the tomb gains in poignancy as the Pope, who has had a series of health problems in recent years, grows older.

The Pope spoke little. After leaving the tomb he thanked a choir that sang as he entered and walked out of the cemetery, and chatted with a group of about 20 nuns who, at a distance, had lent him the comfort of their presence during his prayers.
But at a ceremony a few minutes later, at which John Paul dedicated a new heart surgery unit at a Krakow hospital named after him, he recalled boyhood visits to his brother at work.

The Pope began Monday morning with a private mass in the crypt of the cathedral at Wawel castle, the former seat of Poland's kings. Then he went to the building where he resided as bishop from 1958 to 1964 and another where he spent seven years at the time he was a priest.
The Roman Catholic leader continued to speak out on the most pressing issues of his faith.

At the hospital he praised the many Polish doctors who for reasons of ethics and faith refuse to perform abortions although these were effectively made legal until the 12th week of pregnancy under a reform of Poland's law passed in 1996.

"With my whole heart I praise the doctors, nurses and all Polish health care workers who place the Divine law 'Thou shalt not kill' above what human law allows. I praise you for this witness that you are giving, especially recently," he said.

Later, visiting a Krakow church, the Pope evoked roars of laughter from a crowd when he said: "I just visited a hospital...they told me that they would not admit me, so I just signed the visitors book"
The Pope has been holding up well during the gruelling trip which aides say has invigorated him because of the contact with his compatriots.
A future homecoming by the Pope may not include Krakow, where he spent more than two decades as student, priest, bishop and cardinal.
Later on Monday the Pope was due to fly to the remote southeastern village of Dukla, associated with the Blessed John whom he will make a saint at a mass on Tuesday.
He returns to Rome on Tuesday evening.
